title: The 8-Language Translation Collective Dilemma

scenario.title: The 8-Language Translation Collective Dilemma
scenario.setting: A small, passionate translation collective operates from a cluttered shared office in a former bookstore basement. They translate literary works across 8 underrepresented global languages for a struggling independent small press. Their critical deadline for their first bound anthology is two weeks away, but their funding has suddenly dried up.

characters.name: Kael
characters.tendencies: Tracks all collective budgets, output totals, and billing cycles for the small press partnership

characters.name: Marisol
characters.tendencies: Advocates for preserving linguistic and cultural authenticity in every translation, even if it means adjusting timeline expectations

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: Manages daily collective operations, coordinates between translators and the small press, and trains new volunteer translators

turns.name: Kael
turns.text:
I just pulled up the Q3 billing cycle spreadsheets—we’re still waiting on two freelance translator invoices to come through before we can finalize the royalty payouts for our debut chapbook line. We also just blew past our monthly fundraising target for the new literary translation seed grant, which is a huge win for the collective’s future projects.
[Leans against the cluttered desk, prodding a loose invoice slip tucked under a stack of used poetry translations with his shoe before pulling up a follow-up email draft on his work laptop.]

turns.name: Marisol
turns.text:
"Hold on, let’s hit pause on that quick edit. That regional Oaxacan folk saying the author included isn’t disposable—losing it would strip readers of the exact warmth and local context that makes this story feel alive. We can push back the client’s deadline by a single day, but we can’t get this cultural nuance back once it’s cut."
[She grabs a frayed bilingual anthology from the cluttered desk, flattening the coffee-stained page marked with a sticky note to highlight the phrase in question.]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
Quick check-in, folks—our small press contact just confirmed they’ll drop off advance reader copies of the translated folk zine next week, and I’ve put together a quick training breakdown for our new Portuguese translation volunteer who’s sitting over by the old bookstore shelf of dictionaries. I’m going to pull everyone into a 10-minute sync once we wrap up the first round of poem proofreads.
[I grab a stack of crinkled, annotated translation drafts from the cluttered communal desk and gesture for the group to cluster in the sunlit corner by the stained-glass window.]

turns.name: Kael
turns.text:
I’ve got enough unallocated Q3 reserve to cover the zine’s print fees early without those two pending freelance invoices, so we won’t have to push back the ARC drop-off Javi just confirmed. Let’s circle back to that regional folk saying note from Marisol right after I jot a quick follow-up reminder for the missing invoices.
[Scratches a quick "FOLLOW UP: TRANSLATOR INVOICES 17 & 22" on a neon pink sticky note and presses it to the top of the Q3 spreadsheet stack]

turns.name: Marisol
turns.text:
"Hold on, let’s hit pause on that quick edit. That regional Oaxacan folk saying the author included isn’t disposable—losing it would strip readers of the story’s core cultural warmth and specific community context, not just a throwaway turn of phrase. We can rework our word count elsewhere instead of cutting something that makes this translation feel authentic."
[Grabs a dog-eared Spanish-Zapotec glossary and a pad of translator’s note sticky notes from the cluttered shared desk, nudging a loose stack of translated zine drafts aside to make space]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
Quick check-in, folks—our small press contact just confirmed they’ll drop off advance reader copies of the translated folk zine next week. I also pulled together sign-up sheets for our upcoming volunteer translator training and extra regional dialect glossaries for anyone polishing tricky folk phrasing like the Oaxacan saying Marisol flagged.
[I set the stack of printed materials down between Kael’s open billing spreadsheet and Marisol’s annotated manuscript, then nudged a smudged ceramic yerba maté mug off the cluttered conference table to clear a small work spot.]

dm_opening: DM opening: the cast gathers around a question the scene has been carrying for a year.
dm_closing: DM closing: the Kael holds the line; the next session's hook waits at the door.
